This enables kernel memory manipulation, arbitrary code execution in kernel space, and complete trust zone boundary collapse.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan all device files under /dev for world-readable or world-writable permission bits
how_to_obtain.command: find /dev -type c -o -type b 2>/dev/null | xargs stat --format='%a %n' 2>/dev/null | awk '$1 ~ /[2367]$/ || $1 ~ /^[0-7][0-7][4567]/ {print "WORLD-ACCESSIBLE:", $0}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any output indicates world-accessible device files. Secure systems should produce no output for sensitive devices. Legitimate world-readable devices include /dev/null, /dev/zero, /dev/urandom on most distributions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Specifically check permissions on the highest-risk kernel device nodes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Permissions should be 640 or 660 with owner root and group km, kmem, or equivalent restricted group. Permissions of 644, 664, or 666 indicate world-readable/writable states requiring remediation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use find with permission matching to identify other potentially dangerous world-writable device nodes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Empty output after excluding known-safe devices is the desired secure state. Any device file listed (especially mem, kvm, port, kmem) requires immediate remediation.

typical_values: false (expected on modern distributions; udev defaults restrict sensitive devices to privileged groups)
true (legacy systems, minimalist container base images, or systems where udev has been bypassed or disabled)

option_description: An array listing specific sensitive device node paths (such as /dev/mem, /dev/kmem, /dev/port, /dev/kvm) that have no restrictive ACL entry or udev rule constraining access to root or privileged groups only. Each entry in this list represents a direct kernel ingress path accessible without privilege.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'device_file_ingress_path_to_kernel' when this array has count greater than 0 and udev_device_acl_enforcement_enabled is false. Each device node in this list is a concrete attack surface where an unprivileged process can open a file descriptor to a kernel driver interface, potentially enabling kernel exploits, direct memory reads of credential stores, or hardware-level privilege escalation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check extended ACLs on all sensitive device nodes to identify those without restrictive ACL entries
how_to_obtain.command: for dev in /dev/mem /dev/kmem /dev/port /dev/kvm /dev/raw /dev/nvram /dev/cpu/*/msr 2>/dev/null; do [ -e "$dev" ] && echo "=== $dev ==="; getfacl "$dev" 2>/dev/null; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Each device should show owner: root, group: a privileged group (km, kvm, etc.), and no 'other::r' or 'other::w' entries. Devices showing 'other::r--' or 'other::rw-' should be added to this attribute's list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Enumerate udev rules to identify which sensitive device nodes have explicit ACL rules and which are unprotected
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines matching sensitive device names with GROUP= and MODE= assignments. Devices not appearing in any udev rule with GROUP/MODE restrictions should be added to the sensitive_device_nodes_with_open_acl list.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Generate a combined report of permission and ACL state for all sensitive device nodes to populate the attribute value
how_to_obtain.command: find /dev -type c -o -type b 2>/dev/null | xargs stat --format='%a %U %G %n' 2>/dev/null | awk '{if ($3 == "root" && $1+0 >= 4 && substr($1,length($1)) >= 4) print $4}' | grep -E '(mem|kmem|port|kvm|nvram|msr|raw)'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A list of device paths where the world (other) permission bits allow read or write. This list should directly populate the sensitive_device_nodes_with_open_acl attribute value.

typical_values: [] (empty array; expected on modern hardened distributions with proper udev rules)
['/dev/mem', '/dev/port'] (common on older RHEL/CentOS systems without explicit udev hardening)
['/dev/kvm'] (common in virtualization host environments where KVM access is inadvertently broadened)

option_description: Indicates whether the udev device manager (or equivalent) has active rules that enforce group-based or ACL-based access restrictions on character and block device nodes at device creation time, ensuring that sensitive kernel interface devices are not accessible to unprivileged processes regardless of temporary permission changes.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'device_file_ingress_path_to_kernel' when both device_file_world_readable_writable is true and this attribute is false, and also when sensitive_device_nodes_with_open_acl is non-empty and this is false. Without udev enforcement, even if device permissions are correct at a point in time, a system event, device re-enumeration, or reboot can reset permissions to insecure defaults, repeatedly reopening the kernel ingress path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Verify udevd is running and check for presence of device ACL rules covering sensitive devices
how_to_obtain.command: systemctl is-active systemd-udevd 2>/dev/null || systemctl is-active udevd 2>/dev/null; grep -rE 'SUBSYSTEM=="mem"|KERNEL=="kmem"|KERNEL=="port"|KERNEL=="kvm"|KERNEL=="mem"' /etc/udev/rules.d/ /lib/udev/rules.d/ 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'GROUP|MODE'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: udevd active and matching udev rule lines with GROUP= and MODE= assignments for sensitive devices. If udevd is inactive or no matching rules exist, enforcement is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test that udev rules are actually applied to a specific sensitive device node using udevadm
how_to_obtain.command: udevadm test /sys/class/mem/mem 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'GROUP|MODE|OWNER'; udevadm test /sys/bus/platform/devices/kvm 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'GROUP|MODE|OWNER'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output showing GROUP=km or GROUP=root and MODE=0640 or more restrictive. If udevadm test shows no GROUP/MODE rules applied, enforcement is not effective even if rules appear to exist.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the content of udev rules files to confirm the structure of ACL enforcement rules for kernel device nodes
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rules in the format: KERNEL=="mem", GROUP="km", MODE="0640" for each sensitive device. The presence of GROUP= and MODE= directives in applicable rules confirms ACL enforcement is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Reload and re-trigger udev rules to confirm enforcement is active and rules apply cleanly without errors
how_to_obtain.command: udevadm control --reload-rules 2>/dev/null && udevadm trigger --type=devices 2>/dev/null && journalctl -u systemd-udevd --since '1 minute ago' 2>/dev/null | grep -i error | head -10
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No error output from udevadm and no error messages in the journald output for udevd. Clean reload confirms rules are syntactically valid and actively enforced.

typical_values: true (default on systemd-based modern distributions; udev rules ship with appropriate device restrictions)
false (minimal container base images, systems using devtmpfs without udev, or embedded/custom OS builds where udev is replaced or stripped)
